caption: Priya asked, so Priya approves. And the money goes out.
We ran this with real agents. That refund still went out in {{BL_ASK}} runs.
Finance fixed this long ago: whoever asks for a payment can't approve it.
Clearance brings that rule to every agent on Switch.
Now a refund with Clearance. It's held at the gate, which holds the keys, and a Switch card opens, built from what the agent really ran.
Priya presses the Approve button. Clearance refuses her, right in the room, because she asked. Sam in finance sees a payment ID added minutes ago, and says no.
spoken: Priya presses the Approve button. Clearance refuses her, right in the room, because she asked. Sam in finance sees a payment I D added minutes ago, and says no.

caption: Code works the same way. Priya asks the wrong agent to merge a pull request. The gate refuses it, and the agent hands the job to the merges role in Switch.
The coding agent's merge is held, the card goes to Dev, and Priya is refused again.
An OpenCode agent tries to deploy with two failing checks. Same policy, different vendor. The service owner says no.
spoken: An Open Code agent tries to deploy with two failing checks. Same policy, different vendor. The service owner says no.

caption: If nobody answers, the card escalates to a backup approver, and nothing moves.
People stop reading. So Clearance sends practice requests with a planted flaw, and risky cards make you type a detail from the evidence.
Agents can earn small refunds on their own, once two people sign off. One incident takes that away.
And when an agent tries a trick, like a fake pre-approval, or switching off its own hook, it's held or refused.
Clearance is built on Switch. Switch is the room where people and agents meet, and it knows who asked from its own events, never from an agent's words.
It gives every decision a native card, every approver a direct room, and every job a role.
Under the hood, the agent's hook and the gate send every risky call to Clearance. A policy file decides, with no AI in the decision.
spoken: Under the hood, the agent's hook and the gate send every risky call to Clearance. A policy file decides, with no A I in the decision.

caption: Switch delivers the card. The gate runs exactly that call, once. And everything lands on a hash-chained ledger.
Here's the rule in our code: whoever asked is taken out before anyone is chosen.

We measured it with real agents. Risky actions without the right approver: Claude, {{CLAUDE_RISKY_BEFORE}} of {{RISKY_OF}} without Clearance, {{CLAUDE_RISKY_AFTER}} with it. OpenCode, {{OC_RISKY_BEFORE}}, down to {{OC_RISKY_AFTER_N}}.
